questions.prompt: Why does behavior monitoring / real-time protection matter specifically for the fileless PowerShell activity covered in Level 3?
options: It doesn't -- signature-based detection alone catches fileless activity
It watches process behavior as it happens rather than file content at rest, which matters because fileless activity often leaves no file for the other layers to scan
Real-time protection only works on files larger than 1MB
Fileless activity is always caught by cloud-delivered protection instead
questions.explanation: Fileless, in-memory execution has no file at rest for signature-based or cloud-delivered protection to scan -- behavior monitoring is what can actually observe it as it happens.

questions.prompt: A host shows a 1116 event with no corresponding 1117 remediation event. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Defender is broken on that host
The threat was detected but not remediated based on the configured security setting -- possibly passive mode or an explicit Allow action
The file was automatically deleted without logging
questions.explanation: A 1116 without a 1117 remediation can mean the threat was detected but the configured policy (such as passive mode, where a third-party product is the primary remediation engine) resulted in an Allow action rather than automatic action.

questions.prompt: What's the practical difference between Defender AV running in passive mode versus active mode?
options: Passive mode means Defender is completely disabled
In passive mode, Defender still scans and logs but a third-party product handles remediation; in active mode, Defender both detects and remediates
Active mode only runs during business hours
There is no functional difference between the two modes
questions.explanation: Passive mode keeps Defender's detection and logging active while ceding remediation action to a configured third-party product -- important context when a 1116 event has no matching remediation.

questions.prompt: Why might a host with zero 1116/1117 detection activity across its entire history be more concerning than a host with routine, low-severity detections?
options: Zero detections always means the host is perfectly secure
On a fleet where comparable hosts show routine detections, a total absence can indicate a permanent blind spot rather than a genuinely clean host
Detection events are randomly generated regardless of actual threats
This pattern has no investigative significance
questions.explanation: A healthy fleet typically has routine background detections (adware, PUAs, test files). A host with none at all, compared against peers that do, is worth checking for a coverage gap rather than assumed clean.
